headline: Anthropic's record IPO priced into the worst AI-led selloff in years: the S&P 500 and Dow closed in correction, the Nasdaq had its worst week since 2020, and Nvidia's governance crisis added to the damage. Away from the tape, biotech had a week of mixed trial and FDA news, and private credit got its first official size estimate.

paragraphs.text: The sharpest regulatory story was Capricor. Endpoints and STAT report that the FDA rejected its Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy, deramiocel, for a second time on Friday, even after the company narrowed the indication it was seeking. Endpoints says the agency cited significant problems with the trial, and STAT calls the outcome long expected. Elsewhere on the regulatory calendar, Fierce says the FDA pushed its decision on Belite Bio's rare eye disease pill back three months to May. Sanofi won approval for Infilbray in Gaucher type 3, which Fierce says is the first therapy to address the disease's neurological effects. Fierce also reports the FDA's biologics center is setting up a new body to oversee the post-market safety of vaccines and cell and gene therapies. Separately, Fierce notes the White House pulled its FDA commissioner nomination at the last minute, which leaves leadership at the agency unsettled.

paragraphs.text: In oncology, Merck announced a second positive Phase 3 result for its TROP2 antibody-drug conjugate sacituzumab tirumotecan, this time with an overall survival benefit in gastric or gastroesophageal cancer, per Endpoints and Fierce. Endpoints frames it as helping to offset the coming Keytruda patent cliff. Merck also won legal rounds against Halozyme in the US and Germany over subcutaneous Keytruda Qlex, which Fierce says clears commercialization hurdles. In KRAS, Revolution Medicines posted strong pancreatic data for its pan-RAS drug Rasonque, which BioPharma Dive says is already one of the best oncology launches ever. Challengers are lining up behind it: Erasca is nearing a Phase 3 start, and Alterome presented early Phase 1 data across pancreatic, lung and colon cancers. The data are early, and the competitive pressure on RevMed is the thing to track.

paragraphs.text: The setbacks were in mid-stage trials. Celldex dropped its eczema program after barzolvolimab failed to cut itching versus placebo, and Bausch + Lomb also reported a Phase 2 miss, though Fierce says it is pointing to numerical improvements to argue for Phase 3 talks. Fierce says nChroma halved its headcount and scrapped a hepatitis B trial, and Evaxion is cutting back to oncology only. Novo is trimming another 215 jobs tied to its New Jersey headquarters as it redesigns its US sales organization. Teva's R&D chief and CMO resigned a week after its R&D day, according to Endpoints and Fierce, with an interim replacement in place. Together these suggest capital is going to a few clear winners while the rest of the sector keeps cutting.

paragraphs.text: On deals, STAT reports that Sanofi is weighing a takeover of Insmed, which is one rumor to watch. Pfizer is licensing three in vivo CAR-T programs from China's Starna, and Isomorphic Labs struck a cancer deal with Merck. Marrow Therapeutics launched with a $173 million Series A and B for bone-marrow-targeted genetic medicines. BioPharma Dive says China-sourced assets are heading toward acquisitions or IPOs this year, while Endpoints notes lawmakers in both parties are staking out positions on restricting US investment in Chinese biotech ahead of a Democrat-led Congress. Fierce adds that Adicon's planned $204 million purchase of Crown Biosciences fell through.

paragraphs.text: On the payer and provider side, Kaufman Hall data cited by Healthcare Dive show nearly half of hospitals losing money, with uncompensated care expected to rise as Medicaid changes arrive. CMS proposed Medicare Advantage and Part D changes meant to boost competition, and Fierce says CMS also withdrew its moratorium on new ACA broker registrations. Medicare Advantage insurers are suing over their 2027 star ratings, with UnitedHealth and Aetna named. Medicare accountable care organizations posted a record $2.5 billion in savings in 2025, and CMS wants more participation. TD Cowen sees a UnitedHealth recovery after a three-month slide. Separately, a federal judge approved a $7 billion nationwide Roundup settlement that is expected to end tens of thousands of cancer suits, per the NYT.

paragraphs.text: US stocks ended the week in a rout. The S&P 500 and Dow closed Friday in correction territory, more than 10% below recent highs, and the Nasdaq had its worst week since 2020, according to MarketWatch and the NYT. The WSJ says the Nasdaq is now negative for the year, and the FT describes a tech bear market and the worst week since the Covid crisis. All 11 S&P sectors fell more than 1% on the week for the first time since April 2025, and 94% of index members declined. Chips took the worst of it: MarketWatch puts the weekly wipeout at $2.3 trillion, with a major semiconductor index posting its worst week in 25 years, and the WSJ pegs the broader AI loss near $4 trillion. Treasury yields fell sharply, per the WSJ, a flight-to-safety signal. The WSJ Dollar Index finished the week higher at 98.75. The common thread across outlets is fear over AI capital spending. CNBC reports that prediction-market odds of the S&P reaching 8,000 this year have collapsed from above 70%.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's debut sat in the middle of this. The shares priced into record demand but gave back ground, and the WSJ says they briefly traded only 5 cents above the IPO price on day two. MarketWatch says they held above it, and one comment there calls the failure to hold the opening price bad for tech generally. The FT says the blockbuster debut failed to ease capex worries, and the NYT sees a disconnect between Wall Street and Silicon Valley. CNBC says options list Monday and hedging is likely to be expensive. CNBC also argues the bull market has a supply problem, with companies shifting from buybacks to issuance. Several firms, Seaport among them, are cautious on the stock.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia is the other pressure point. The FT and NYT report the SEC is probing its accounting, after questions surfaced around questionable chip sales in Asia and Jensen Huang's resignation. MarketWatch says the stock has lost $1.16 trillion in seven sessions, its worst weekly losing stretch since 2008, and one fund manager warns that uncertainty leaves it open to more selling. Lawmakers released information showing Commerce approved sales of more than 800,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, some with military ties, per the NYT. The NYT also links Alice Huang, accused of spying on Nvidia's CEO, to firms tied to China's military. The WSJ calls Huang's no-contract handshake deals a red flag, and Bloomberg says Trump wants Huang to apologize and return, which it calls highly unlikely. Elsewhere, MarketWatch says memory-chip stocks look cheap but analysts read that as a peak-cycle warning, and Take-Two's stock has shrugged off GTA 6.

paragraphs.text: Beyond tech, Trump threatened a tax on data centers built outside the US, per the FT and NYT, though the NYT says it is unclear how he would carry it out. On rates, Fed governor Lisa Cook said skipping an October hike risked leaving the Fed behind on inflation, while CNBC says Chair Warsh wants officials to talk less and they are talking more. The WSJ says next week's flash PMIs may show whether central banks can raise rates further, and the FT reports October inflation keeps the Bank of Japan on a tightening path. Eurozone negotiated wage growth ticked up to 2.57%. Michigan sentiment improved but remains low, and Canadian retail sales are heading for their sharpest drop in more than a year and a half.

paragraphs.text: Coverage was light on hard credit news, but there was a notable data point. ABF Journal reports private credit has received its first official count, putting it at 7.1% of corporate debt. The report does not say who produced the figure, so treat it with caution. It matters because regulators have lacked a measure of the market's size as the AI selloff and tightening central banks raise questions about borrower health.

FIN News says a West Coast pension approved pacing plans for private equity and private credit. In structured credit, Fitch assigned ratings to Anthelion CLO 4, a $400 million US leveraged loan portfolio, a sign the primary market is still functioning.

Both bear on credit if rate hikes stay on the table. The WSJ notes that Treasury yields plunged on the day, which helps duration but suggests risk aversion.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO is the story of the week, and there is a lot of colour around it. CNBC puts the offering at $81 billion, and the NYT and WSJ call it the biggest IPO ever. The FT's Alphaville ran a postmortem on how the market cap compared with its pre-IPO guess. Ark Invest bought $90.8 million across six funds, per CNBC, and Cathie Wood says she is quite optimistic. The FT's Markets desk raises the small-float issue, noting that big IPOs are coming with small floats. MarketWatch warns that billions of locked-up shares could weigh on the stock over the next year. The deal also tests the IPO window, and weak aftermarket trading would affect other issuers.
